How to check a token or link for scams before you touch it

Most crypto losses come from a handful of repeated tricks, not from clever hacking. A few minutes of checking before you click, connect or buy helps you avoid many of them.

Red flags that mean stop

  • Someone promises guaranteed or very high returns, or says “risk free”.
  • A stranger, a “support agent” or an “admin” messages you first, especially on Telegram, WhatsApp or X.
  • You are told to hurry: “last chance”, “only today”, “spots almost gone”.
  • Anyone asks for your seed phrase, private key or a screenshot of your wallet. Real services never do.
  • A token you never bought appears in your wallet and a site invites you to “claim” or sell it.
  • The link came from a chat message, a pop-up or an ad, not from the project's official website.

Five checks, in order

  1. Find the official address yourself. Get the project's website from CoinGecko or from its verified social account, then type the address in your browser. Copying a link from a chat is how fake sites catch people.
  2. Read the link letter by letter. Fake sites use near-identical spellings, extra words or a different ending, such as .xyz instead of .com.
  3. Scan the token contract. Paste the contract address into a scanner such as GoPlus. Warning signs include a honeypot (you can buy but not sell), very high buy or sell taxes, and an owner who can create new tokens or change the rules.
  4. Look at who holds the token. On a block explorer, open the holders list. If a few wallets hold most of the supply, they can sell and crash the price.
  5. Review what you approve. Connecting a wallet is not the same as signing. Read every approval, avoid “unlimited” approvals, and revoke old ones you no longer use.

What a clean scan does not tell you

A scanner finds known patterns. It cannot see a team that plans to disappear, and new scams are made to pass scans. Treat a clean result as one input, not as permission. Nothing on this page predicts whether a token will rise or fall.

If you already clicked or signed something

  • Stop interacting with the site. Do not type your seed phrase anywhere to “fix” the problem.
  • If you entered your seed phrase or private key anywhere, treat that wallet as compromised: create a new wallet on a clean device and move what remains.
  • Revoke token approvals for the old wallet.
  • Report the scam to the exchange or platform involved and to your local police or cybercrime unit. Keep screenshots and transaction IDs.
  • Be careful with anyone who offers to “recover” your money for a fee. This is a very common second scam.
